sentences.text: This long-snouted crocodile inhabited much of Africa throughout the Neogene period.
It evolved its elongated snout independently of other crocodilians, indicating a diet focused on fish.
The skull displays deeply scalloped edges on the front bones and gaps between the teeth, creating a saw-like appearance when viewed from above.
Its dentition consisted of slender, pointed teeth with two ridges, clearly adapted for catching fish.
Unlike most other crocodilians, this animal typically possessed only four teeth in the front bones of the upper jaw.
A prominent ridge on the nasal bone led toward the eyes, forming a sloping forehead similar to that of Crocodylus checchiai.
Fossils found at Lothagam show that this species coexisted with up to four different species of crocodiles.
The genus was established by Fourtau in 1920.
Three recognized species exist within the genus: E. nitriae, E. brumpti, and E. arambourgi.
Ginsburg and Buffetaut described a third species, Euthecodon arambourgi, in 1978 from a skull found in Gebel Zelten, Libya.
Euthecodon arambourgi lived during the Burdigalian stage of the Miocene.
Euthecodon arambourgi was described based on remains found in the Miocene of Libya and Egypt.
Euthecodon brumpti was originally described from fossil material in the Omo Basin of Ethiopia dating to the Pliocene to Pleistocene.
Fossils of Euthecodon brumpti have been found at localities including Lothagam, Kanapoi, Longarakak, Nakoret, and Todenyang.
There are 57 recorded fossil occurrences of Euthecodon.
Euthecodon shows a series of adaptations that are present in E. arambourgi, exaggerated in E. nitriae, and peak in E. brumpti.
The eyes face more forward in later species of Euthecodon than in E. arambourgi.
Euthecodon has notably small supratemporal fossae, creating a weak insertion point for jaw musculature.
Despite its unique dental adaptations, Euthecodon likely had a relatively weak bite.
The piscivorous and aquatic lifestyle of Euthecodon was perfected in E. brumpti during the Pliocene to Pleistocene.
Euthecodon and Eogavialis were heavily specialized for a piscivorous diet, preying on smaller fish.
Euthecodon's specialized lifestyle may have prevented it from venturing into saltwater, restricting it to riverbanks further upstream.
Increased aridification, salinity, and conditions favoring temporary water bodies may have contributed to the disappearance of the highly specialized Euthecodon.
Later research shows that Euthecodon's resemblance to gavialoids is due to convergent evolution, placing it deeper within the Crocodylidae.
Euthecodon differs from gavialids and tomistomines by having small supratemporal fossae and a relatively gradual narrowing of the rostrum.
Most current analyses place Euthecodon in Osteolaeminae, a family including the dwarf crocodile, Rimasuchus, Brochuchus, Voay, and the slender-snouted crocodile.
Phylogenetic analysis identifies Mecistops as a close relative of Euthecodon.
Euthecodon belongs to the subfamily Euthecodontini.
Euthecodon lived from the Aquitanian to the Late Pleistocene, between 23.04 and 0.0117 million years ago.
Moghara and Gebel Zelten preserve fluvio-marine environments with fossils of sharks, dolphins, sawfish, catfish, anthracotheres, carnivorans, proboscideans, and primates.
Researchers debated whether the initial species described by Joleaud and Fourtau were distinct enough to be separate species.
Variations in tooth counts have led some researchers to question whether certain specimens assigned to E. brumpti represent a distinct species.
A 2017 publication by Christopher Brochu suggests that many Miocene to Pliocene remains from the Turkana Basin may belong to an unnamed species rather than E. brumpti.
Researchers have suggested that Euthecodon brumpti might be a junior synonym of E. nitriae.
Some traits in Euthecodon do not follow a direct evolutionary series and appear most prominent in the intermediate species E. nitriae.
